                     MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                               GERONIMO POWER, LLC

         Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”

or “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Geronimo Power, LLC (“Geronimo Power”)

hereby files this answer2 in response to the reply briefs filed by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

(“PJM”)3 and the PJM Transmission Owners4 in the above-captioned proceedings.




         1
            18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213.
         2
            Rule 213(a)(3) allows for an answer to be submitted to “any pleading, if not prohibited under paragraph
(a)(2) of this section.” 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(3). Paragraph (a)(2) does not prohibit answers to briefs or reply briefs.
Nevertheless, out of an abundance of caution, Geronimo Power moves for leave to file this answer. The Commission
has accepted answers in the past when they have (i) assisted the Commission in understanding the issues presented,
(ii) provided additional information for the Commission’s decision-making process, and (iii) helped ensure an accurate
record. See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 181 FERC ¶ 61,162, at P 29 (2022); Canal Generating LLC, 181
FERC ¶ 61,157, at P 14 (2022); Equitrans, L.P., 134 FERC ¶ 61,250, at P 6 (2011); Cal. Indep. Sys. Operator Corp.,
132 FERC ¶ 61,023, at P 16 (2010). In this proceeding, Geronimo Power’s answer will help the Commission
understand the issues presented in this proceeding and provide further information to inform the Commission’s
decision-making process. Geronimo Power therefore respectfully requests leave to file this answer to the extent the
Commission deems such leave is necessary and requests that the Commission consider this answer in its deliberations
in this proceeding.

 I.       ANSWER

         At the heart of the Commission’s Show Cause Order5 lies a recognition that the current

paradigm for serving large loads in PJM is not sufficiently flexible to accommodate the growth of

hyperscale data centers and other large load customers that are essential for the nation’s economic

prosperity, national security, and global competitiveness. As the Show Cause Order explained,

the current framework for serving large loads within PJM requires that large loads that “are willing

and able to limit their energy withdrawals from the transmission system” nevertheless pay for

“costly and inefficient transmission system buildout that may not be necessary” to serve them.6

And because, as stated by Commissioner Rosner in his concurrence to the Show Cause Order, it

“has become persistently difficult and increasingly expensive to build new grid infrastructure in

this country,”7 large loads are simply unable to timely obtain service even if they are willing to

pay for transmission system upgrades.

         The Commission sought to remedy this situation by ordering PJM to adopt three new

transmission services—Interim Network Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”), Firm

Contact Demand, and Non-Firm Contract Demand—that would reflect that certain large loads

which co-locate with generation resources are able and willing to limit their reliance on the PJM

transmission system.8 But the positions taken by PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners in their

briefs filed in this proceeding regarding how these new transmission services will be implemented

transmission service that requires fewer Network Upgrades to provide.”).

         8

transmission services that reflect Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of Co-Located Loads that are willing
and able to limit their energy withdrawals from the transmission system under certain conditions.”).

                                                         2
 will, if adopted, have the effect of preserving the status quo in PJM. More specifically, certain

rates, terms, and conditions proposed by PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners associated with

these new transmission services will effectively limit the ability of large load customers to take

transmission service that reflects their actual grid usage, disincentivize large loads from entering

into flexible co-location arrangements that minimize their impact on the grid, delay the timeline

for large loads to obtain the service they require, and lead to inefficient transmission build out.

       Geronimo Power urges the Commission to reject any rates, terms, and conditions proposed

by PJM or the PJM Transmission Owners that unnecessarily limit the flexibility of large loads to

co-locate and take transmission service based on their actual use of the grid consistent with the

Show Cause Order. Geronimo Power files this answer to highlight the positions of PJM and the

PJM Transmission Owners that are inconsistent with the flexibility the Show Cause Order

envisioned and, if adopted, would be most detrimental to the Commission’s efforts to ensure that

large loads can be served efficiently, reliably, and on a timeline that ensures the U.S. does not fall

behind in the industries of the future.

       A.         The Commission Should Reject PJM’s And The PJM Transmission Owners’
                  Proposals To Restrict Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service To
                  Outages

       In its Reply, PJM doubles down on its view that Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission

service should be limited to when a generation facility is on “outage or temporary derate

conditions…”9 The PJM Transmission Owners take this one step further by saying that Non-Firm

Contract Demand transmission service should only be available “when a generator is offline due

to a breakdown or maintenance issues” and should “not cover other instances when a generator is

not operating, such as when intermittent generation resources are unable to produce; when a co-



       9
           PJM Reply at 7.

                                                  3
 located battery has depleted its available energy; or when a natural gas generator is unable to secure

fuel.”10 These proposed restrictions on Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service are

inconsistent with the requirements of the Show Cause Order, will unnecessarily restrict the ability

of large loads to co-locate, and should be rejected by the Commission.

       As an initial matter, restricting Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service to when

a co-located generation facility is on outage is inconsistent with the requirements of the Show

Cause Order. In the Show Cause Order, the Commission explained that “not all Co-Located Loads

will necessarily plan to withdraw energy from the transmission system on a regular basis” and thus

Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service should be available for when such loads “seek

to withdraw energy from the transmission system from time to time when transmission capacity is

available and not needed by firm customers.”11 Moreover, the Commission indicated that Non-

Firm Contract Demand transmission service should “be available only when there is available

transmission capacity, similar to existing non-firm transmission service options in the Tariff … for

terms ranging from one hour to one month…”12 The Commission in no way suggested that it

would be appropriate to limit the availability of Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service

to times when co-located resources are on outage.

       PJM’s and the PJM Transmission’s Owners’ proposals to restrict Non-Firm Contract

Demand transmission service to when a co-located resource is on outage ignores the requirements

for this service outlined in the Show Cause Order. Rather than making Non-Firm Contract

Demand transmission service available for co-located loads at any time when transmission

capacity is available, PJM has proposed unnecessary restrictions that will limit co-located load


       10
          PJM TO Reply at 6.
       11
          Show Cause Order at P 214.
       12
          Id. at P 215.

                                                  4
 from relying on the grid even when excess grid capacity is available to serve them. This is not the

flexibility that the Show Cause Order envisioned that Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission

service would provide.

       The restrictions imposed by PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners on Non-Firm Contract

Demand transmission service would fundamentally undermine a key benefit of co-location.

Specifically, a primary reason that large loads are considering co-location is so that they can reduce

their impact on the grid and, in turn, obtain speed to power on a timeline that traditional utilities

are increasingly proving unable to accommodate. Large loads’ efforts to reduce their impact on

the grid through co-location may take on a variety of forms, including the use of intermittent

resources paired with natural gas or battery energy storage or reducing their load (i.e., curtailing)

at times of high demand when non-firm service is unavailable.

       For example, a solar and battery hybrid facility or natural gas generator may have the ability

to meet the needs of co-located load in all but a limited set of hours during a year (e.g., due to

unexpected natural gas supply interruptions). Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service

was intended to provide such a customer the option to obtain transmission service on an as-

available basis to meet its load during those limited instances where the onsite generation resource

is unavailable to meet its demand (subject to an obligation to curtail if transmission service is

unavailable).

       Yet, under PJM and the PJM Transmission Owner’s proposal, co-located load effectively

would have no alternative to taking NITS or Firm Contract Demand transmission service for its

entire demand to ensure that it is able to obtain service during the limited handful of hours when

the generation resource is unavailable for reasons other than a “breakdown or maintenance




                                                  5
 issues.”13 In effect, PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal would force a co-located

load that is able to meet its own demand in all but a handful of hours to be studied as if it is planning

to rely exclusively on the grid to serve its needs. Inevitably, these studies will lead to the

conclusion that accommodating these loads requires the construction of costly new transmission

upgrades—upgrades that would be avoided if the customer is given the flexibility to take non-firm

service during the limited periods when the onsite generation is unavailable.

         PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners’ primary rationale for imposing this restriction

appears to be that making Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service more broadly available

poses reliability concerns since the PJM system has not been planned to accommodate this load.14

But this misses the entire point of this service. In the Show Cause Order the Commission made

clear that Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service “would be available only when there

is available transmission capacity” and that co-located loads using such service “would not be

considered for resource adequacy planning purposes.”15 When transmission capacity is not

available, large loads relying on Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service will be

curtailed.16 PJM thus does not need to expand its transmission system or otherwise change its

operations to accommodate this load; it merely needs to allow such load to take transmission

service when it is available, as PJM itself acknowledges.17 If transmission service is unavailable

         17

conditions at the time of the request and any constraints that may arise regarding energy and reliability. For energy,

 during particular periods, then the customer will be forced to curtail. If the system conditions that

impose reliability risks arise, PJM can refuse to accommodate requests for this non-firm service.

And to the extent that accommodating this service would require PJM to make changes to its

markets and operations systems as PJM claims,18 that should not be a barrier to providing co-

located loads the flexibility the Commission required of PJM in the Show Cause Order.

        The effect of PJM and PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal will be to severely limit co-

location opportunities in PJM. Large loads will either need to co-locate with a resource that can

be called upon at all times (other than when on outage) even when there is excess grid capacity to

serve them or take NITS or Firm Contract Demand transmission service that will result in the same

inefficient, timely, and costly grid build out that undermines speed to power efforts that the Show

Cause Order sought to avoid. The Commission should not allow PJM and the PJM Transmission

Owners to prolong the status quo in PJM by depriving large loads of the flexibility the Show Cause

Order was clearly intended to afford.

        B.       The PJM Transmission Owners Have Not Demonstrated That Charging The
                 Same Rate For Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service As Firm
                 Transmission Service Is Just And Reasonable

        No party in this proceeding disputes that Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service

is a lesser service than NITS or Firm Contract Demand transmission service. Non-Firm Contract

Demand transmission service can be taken only on an as-available basis and is subject to

curtailment before NITS or Firm Contract Demand transmission service. Yet despite the fact that

Non-Firm Contact Demand transmission service is indisputably an inferior service, the PJM


the Co-Located Generating Facility’s outage may coincide with high demand conditions on the Transmission System
or where system conditions otherwise (e.g., seasonal outages) may not allow such transmission service or energy to
be offered reliably.”).
         18
            Id. (“In Essence, Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service is intended to provide whatever level
of service the Transmission System can reliably accommodate at that snapshot in time without any advanced planning
for transmission or capacity.”).

                                                        7
 Transmission Owners have proposed to apply the same rate they charge for NITS and Firm

Contract Demand transmission service to Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service. The

PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal is unjust and unreasonable, will disincentivize co-located

loads from relying on Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service, and lead to less efficient

use of the transmission system.

        Neither the PJM Transmission Owners nor any other party to this proceeding have provided

a reasonable basis for the Commission to conclude that it is just and reasonable to apply the same

NITS or Firm Contract Demand transmission service rate to Non-Firm Contract Demand

transmission service. The PJM Transmission Owners have instead simply restated their flawed

initial rationales for charging the same rate for an inferior service. For example, the PJM

Transmission Owners explain that it would be inappropriate for them to apply the non-firm point-

to-point transmission rate to Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service because such

service is “demonstrably superior” to non-firm point-to-point transmission service.19 But as

Geronimo Power explained in its Response,20 the question before the Commission is not whether

the PJM Transmission Owners should charge the non-firm point-to-point transmission rate for

Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service. The question is what is a just and reasonable

rate for Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service. The PJM Transmission Owners have

offered no meaningful response to this question.

        The PJM Transmission Owners also reiterate that Commission policy allows them to

charge up to the same rate they charge for firm transmission service and that such rate is justified

until they “gather data on how Non-Firm Contract Demand Service customers are utilizing the



        19
            Id. at 19.
        20
            PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al., Response Brief of Geronimo Power, LLC
at 7 (Mar. 25, 2026) (“Geronimo Response”).

                                                      8
 service, taking into account the intended purpose of the service, and the effect of that utilization

on the system.”21 But, as Geronimo Power noted in its Response,22 the mere fact that Commission

policy allows the PJM Transmission Owners to charge up to the firm rate in some cases, does not

mean that doing so here is just and reasonable. And the Commission itself has acknowledged that

rates for non-firm service generally should be lower than the rates for firm service.23 The PJM

Transmission Owners have provided no independent basis for the Commission to conclude it is

just and reasonable to charge the same rate for Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service

as they charge for NITS and Firm Contract Demand transmission service.

        Moreover, while the PJM Transmission Owners claim that “it is far from certain what

upgrades may be required for Non-Firm Contract Demand Service customers” and thus assert that

they cannot yet determine the appropriate discount they should provide to Non-Firm Contract

Demand transmission customers,24 there should be little doubt that some form of discount must be

applied. This is particularly true given that the Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service

the Show Cause Order contemplates is required to be offered only when the PJM system is capable

of accommodating such service. Because Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service is

offered on an as-available basis the extent to which network upgrades are required for Non-Firm

Contract Demand transmission service—to the extent any are required at all—should be minimal

(assuming that reasonable study assumptions are applied).25

be accommodated without network upgrades will likely depend on how the co-located loads taking this service are
studied. For instance, there could be scenarios where overly conservative study assumptions result in network

          C.       The PJM Transmission Owners Have Not Demonstrated That Their Proposed
                  Grid Reliance Charge Is Just And Reasonable And Consistent With Cost
                  Causation Requirements

         Geronimo Power does not oppose the concept of a Grid Reliance Charge. Indeed, despite

accusations to the contrary by the PJM Transmission Owners,26 Geronimo Power made clear in its

Response that “it may be appropriate to impose certain charges on co-located load for

demonstrated costs they cause and benefits that accrue to them” but maintained that any such

charge must be based on co-located loads’ actual impact on the grid and the transmission services

they receive consistent with the Federal Power Act’s (“FPA”) cost causation requirements.27 The

PJM Transmission Owners’ Initial Brief neither demonstrated that a Grid Reliance Charge is

necessary in this case nor that their proposed Grid Reliance Charge accurately reflects co-located

loads’ actual grid impact or the transmission service they will receive. And the PJM Transmission

Owners’ Reply fairs no better. The PJM Transmission Owners instead simply reiterate two of

their three flawed rationales for applying a Grid Reliance Charge that would currently be 25.8%

of a transmission owners’ annual transmission revenue requirement to all co-located load relying

on onsite generation.




upgrades being triggered to accommodate a request for Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service. But such
study scenarios would likely be based on unnecessarily conservative study assumptions regarding the level of service
requested (e.g., an assumption that a co-located load would take this service 95% of the time) that do not reflect how
this type of service is likely to be taken nor align with the level of service directed by the Commission for Non-Firm
Contract Demand transmission service. Such conservative study assumptions for Non-Firm Contract Demand
transmission service are neither required nor appropriate. Rather, they would result in unnecessary network upgrades
and inefficient system planning that would discourage parties from entering into flexible co-location arrangements
that rely on Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service and ultimately undermine the Commission’s goal of
providing alternative speed to power options for large loads while mitigating grid impacts. The Commission should
require PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners to clearly articulate their approach to studying large loads requesting
Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service so that it can determine whether the network upgrades PJM and the
PJM Transmission Owners claim Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service will cause are not the mere result
of unrealistic study assumptions.
          26
             PJM TO Reply at 22 (“Vistra and Geronimo are the only two parties that suggest no Grid Reliance Charge
is necessary.”).
          27
             Geronimo Response at 9-10.

                                                         10
          First, the PJM Transmission Owners restate their position that the delivery of black start

and regulation services justify their proposed Grid Reliance Charge because these services

“provide no value without the ability to access the transmission system to obtain them.”28 But the

fact that these services provide no value to load that is not interconnected to the transmission

system does not mean that there is a delivery cost associated with the provision of these services.

Indeed, as Geronimo Power explained in its Response, neither black start nor regulation service

include a delivery component and the PJM Transmission Owners have not sought to impose such

delivery charge on other transmission customers.29 The PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal to

assess a charge for the delivery of black start and regulation service when other customers are not

required to pay a separate delivery charge is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory and

preferential.

         The Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative, Inc. (“NOVEC”) attempts to justify the PJM

Transmission Owners’ proposal by noting that although “the current formula for Black Start

Service does not include a delivery component,” that “simply reflects the fact that all load besides

Co-Located Load in PJM would otherwise cover the cost of transmission service required for

Black Start Service.”30 NOVEC overlooks, however, that co-located loads taking Non-Firm

Contract Demand transmission service also will contribute to grid costs through the charges that

they pay for this service. Additionally, PJM has proposed to assess co-located load charges for

black start and regulation service on a gross basis.31 It is thus unclear why co-located load should

of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners to Paper Hearing Questions at 18-19 (April 24, 2026).

                                                         11
 have to pay for black start and regulation service as all other transmission customers do and pay a

separate delivery charge for these services that is not assessed to any other customers.

       Second, the PJM Transmission Owners also reiterate their claim that being connected to

the grid provides co-located load with “obvious benefits” which they explain include “frequency

support, inertia, voltage stability, fault current capability, ride-through and protections

coordination, and providing sufficient short-circuit capability.”32 But the PJM Transmission

Owners have not demonstrated that these benefits will accrue to the same degree for co-located

load that is being primarily supplied by onsite generation. And there is no evidence in this

proceeding that these benefits alone justify applying a charge that is based on the percentage of

transmission depreciation and operations and maintenance expense of a transmission owner’s

annual transmission revenue requirement (currently 25.8%) to all co-located load relying on onsite

generation.33

       Applying a Grid Reliance Charge to all co-located loads that bears no relationship to their

impact on the grid and the services they receive is not only inconsistent with the FPA, but will

discourage co-location arrangements. While large loads are prepared to pay their fair share of grid

charges and certain large loads may even be willing to pay more if it can accelerate their timeline

to service, imposing a Grid Reliance Charge that is not reflective of the benefits co-located loads

receive will disincentivize co-location arrangements. Requiring customers that make significant

investments to bring their own co-located resource online to also pay a Grid Reliance Charge that

is over a quarter of PJM transmission owners’ annual revenue requirement and for which they do

not receive a corresponding benefit could render the co-location calculus uneconomic for many




       32

       33

                                                12
 large loads. Indeed, a charge that is divorced from the benefits co-located load receives may

incentivize these loads to simply elect NITS or Firm Contract Demand transmission service if there

is no cost difference between those services and the Non-Firm Contract Demand option, which, in

turn, undermines the goal of supporting the timely interconnection of large loads and will lead to

inefficient and unnecessary grid build out. The Commission should decline to allow the PJM

Transmission Owners to impose any form of Grid Reliance Charge on co-located load until they

demonstrate that such charge is necessary, consistent with the FPA’s cost causation requirements,

and will not disincentivize large loads to co-locate.

II.    CONCLUSION

       Geronimo Power respectfully requests that the Commission issue an order consistent with

its filings in these proceedings.
